title: Know the Design, and You Will Know the Designer
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: In the fall of 1941, Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral came home from a hunting trip in the Alps with his dog, both of them covered in burdock burrs. Instead of brushing them off, he put one under a microscope. He saw hundreds of springy little hooks catching on every loop of fabric. After years of trial and error, he patented the hook-and-loop fastener we know today as Velcro. He didn’t invent it. He noticed it and copied it.

That is how an entire field works. It’s called biomimicry: learning from nature. Japan’s bullet train used to burst out of tunnels with a boom that woke people hundreds of yards away, until one of the engineers, a bird-watcher in his spare time, gave the nose the shape of a kingfisher’s beak, because that bird dives into water with barely a splash. The boom disappeared, the train got faster, and it uses less electricity. Self-cleaning glass was copied from the lotus leaf, and an office building cooled without conventional air conditioning was copied from a termite mound. Pound for pound, spider silk is stronger than steel, except that steel requires a mill and a thousand degrees, while a spider spins at body temperature, from protein and water. Engineers don’t copy weak solutions. They copy the ones that beat their own.

But the most finely crafted design of all is the one you carry inside you. In nearly every cell of your body lies a six-foot strand of DNA holding the blueprint for all of you, packed more densely than any hard drive can manage. Your heart will beat a hundred thousand times today and keep it up for decades without a service appointment. Your brain runs on about as much energy as a dim light bulb. Your skin stitches up its own cuts.

Psychology says that being amazed by all this is not a luxury. It’s health. Regular awe lowers stress, quiets the hamster wheel of our thoughts, and makes us kinder. And it can be practiced. Take a fifteen-minute walk without your phone, with one task: find something along the way that you can’t explain.

That leaves a question. The Velcro patent bears the inventor’s signature. What about the burdock’s hooks? The Bible answers simply: when you get to know the design, you get to know the Designer. And it adds the most personal thing of all: you, too, are His handiwork, not a mistake and not an accident.

quote.text: I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well.

questions: When was the last time something truly amazed you?
What would change in the way you see yourself if you believed you were someone’s handiwork and not an accident?

paragraphs: In the fall of 1941, Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral came home from a hunting trip in the Alps with his dog. His pants and the dog’s fur were covered in burdock burrs. Most of us would have brushed them off in irritation and forgotten about it. De Mestral did something else: he put one burr under a microscope. He saw hundreds of tiny, springy hooks that caught on every loop of fabric and every tuft of fur. He figured that if something held on that well, it could be reproduced. After years of trial and error, he patented a fastener made of two strips: one with hooks, the other with loops. He called it Velcro. Today Velcro fastens children’s shoes all over the world, astronauts’ suits, and surgeons’ gowns.

It’s worth noticing what actually happened here. De Mestral didn’t invent anything. He noticed something. The solution already existed, refined down to the last detail, and it stuck to his pants. The engineer simply copied it.

This isn’t an isolated story. It’s an entire way of working, and it has a name: biomimicry, learning from nature. Japan’s Shinkansen bullet train once had a serious problem. As it exited a tunnel, compressed air shot out ahead of it with a boom that woke people hundreds of yards away. The engineering team was led by a man who watched birds in his spare time. He remembered the kingfisher, a bird that dives from the air into the water with barely a splash, because its long, wedge-shaped beak slices smoothly through the boundary between air and water instead of ramming into it. The front of the train was redesigned in the shape of a kingfisher’s beak. The boom disappeared, and along the way the train became faster and started using less electricity.

There are hundreds of stories like this. A lotus leaf is never dirty, even though the plant grows in mud. Its surface is covered with microscopic bumps that make water droplets roll off like little balls, carrying the dirt with them. Self-cleaning exterior paints and windows work on the same principle today. In Africa, termites build mounds in which the temperature stays nearly constant, even though it’s scorching outside by day and cool at night. An architect designing an office building in Harare borrowed their system of channels and chimneys and put up a building that does without conventional air conditioning, using a fraction of the energy its neighboring high-rises need. And spider silk? Pound for pound, it’s stronger than steel. To make steel, we need a steel mill and more than a thousand degrees. A spider spins its thread at ordinary temperature, from protein and water, silently and on the spot.
Notice one thing: engineers don’t copy weak solutions. They copy the ones that beat their own. The best laboratories in the world go to nature the way apprentices go to a master.

The most interesting part, though, is that you don’t have to go to Japan or Africa to find the most finely crafted design of all. You carry it inside you. In nearly every cell of your body lies a strand of DNA about six feet long, coiled so ingeniously that it fits inside the cell’s nucleus, which you can’t even see with the naked eye. Written on that strand, in a four-letter chemical alphabet, are the assembly and operating instructions for all of you. No drive built by human hands stores information so densely or so durably. Your heart will beat about a hundred thousand times today. It will do the same tomorrow and the day after, for decades, with no maintenance and no replacement parts, adjusting its own pace to running, sleep, and emotion. Your brain, a network of tens of billions of nerve cells, does work that would put computing centers to shame, and it draws about as much energy as a single dim light bulb. Your eye focuses itself, cleans itself, and moves smoothly from the glare of noon to the dark of night. With every jump, your bones bear several times your body weight, and yet your whole skeleton weighs only a couple dozen pounds. When you cut your skin, it stitches itself back together, and your blood clots exactly where it needs to. If any company built a device with specs like these, its engineers would be collecting awards for the rest of their lives.

You can shrug all this off: just ordinary biology. Most of us do exactly that, and no wonder, because the brain is built to push things that are constant and familiar into the background. It’s a useful mechanism; thanks to it we don’t analyze the doorknob every morning. But it comes at a price: over the years we stop seeing the wonders we brush up against every day. Water from the tap. Speech. Spring. Our own hands.

Children can still do it. A four-year-old asks dozens of questions a day, and nearly every one starts with “why.” Why is grass green? Why does the moon follow us? Then school, work, and hurry teach us that asking isn’t appropriate and there’s no time to wonder. Too often we mistake adulthood for indifference. Yet the capacity for wonder isn’t something childish we outgrow. It’s a skill we lose. And if it can be lost, it can also be regained.

This is where psychology has more and more to say. For about twenty years, science has been systematically studying a state it calls awe: what we feel when we stand before something bigger than anything we had imagined. Researchers have found that the average person experiences such moments two or three times a week, but rarely notices them and almost never names them. They have also listed the main sources of awe: nature, music, art, big ideas, birth and death, spiritual experiences, the shared exhilaration of a crowd, and, perhaps most surprising of all, moral beauty, the sight of someone’s courage, kindness, and faithfulness. Watching a person act nobly produces the same responses in the body as the sight of a starry sky.

And the effects are measurable. Awe calms the nervous system and lowers markers of inflammation. It quiets the constant inner monologue, that hamster wheel of tasks, judgments, and worries. Researchers talk about the “small self” effect: when we look at something that dwarfs us, our grievances shrink back to their proper size, and in their place comes a sense of belonging to something bigger. Right after a moment of awe, people are measurably more generous and kind. They also feel as if they have more time. In short, wonder is not a luxury for poets. It’s health.

The trouble is that awe has powerful competition these days. The screen serves up a new image every second, so none of them has time to amaze us. But wonder doesn’t disappear because the world has become ordinary. It disappears because we have stopped looking. The good news: looking can be trained like a muscle.

Here are three simple tools to start with. The first is an awe walk. Fifteen minutes, phone in your pocket, and one single task: find something along the way that you can’t explain. A bud on a branch. A spider by a streetlight. The shape of a cloud. Walk down your own street like a tourist seeing it for the first time. The second tool is the question “How does this actually work?” Ask it of things you’ve taken for granted for years. How does a bee know where the hive is? How does your hand tell silk from paper before you even have time to think? You don’t need to know the answer, because the question itself shakes you out of numbness. The third is an awe journal. In the evening, write one sentence about one thing that amazed you that day. People who do this regularly report, after a few weeks, a calmer mind and a warmer view of others. And if you have children or grandchildren, there’s a fourth tool, the most enjoyable one: show them what you’ve discovered, and let them show you something too. Shared awe grows.

In the end, we are left with a question that’s hard to set aside. The Velcro patent has a number, a date, and the owner’s name. The solution de Mestral copied from the burdock has no signature on file in any patent office. The train with the kingfisher’s beak was designed by a specific team whose names are known. And the kingfisher’s beak itself? When we read a sentence that makes sense, it never occurs to us that the letters arranged themselves. When an engineer finds a solution in nature that beats his own, he copies it with admiration. Science does a wonderful job of describing how it all works, and we owe it gratitude for that. But the question of where the idea came from remains open. For centuries it was wonder that drove people to study the world: many great scientists treated nature as a book worth reading carefully, because someone had written it.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: For decades, engineers have been copying solutions they spotted in nature: Velcro came from the burdock, the nose of a bullet train from the kingfisher’s beak, self-cleaning glass from the lotus leaf, and an energy-efficient office building from a termite mound. The nearest example of such finely crafted design is your own body: DNA stores information more densely than any hard drive, the heart beats for decades without servicing, the brain runs on the power of a light bulb, and the skin stitches up its own cuts. Psychology adds that the capacity to be amazed by all this is not a luxury but health: regular awe lowers stress, quiets the hamster wheel of our thoughts, and makes us kinder. It can be practiced with three tools: an awe walk, the question “How does this actually work?” and one sentence of awe written down in the evening.

sections.heading: Look Higher
paragraphs: From its first pages, the Bible speaks of the world as a work of design, not an accident. The apostle Paul wrote that God’s invisible qualities have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, understood from what He has made. In other words: when you get to know the design, you get to know the Designer. So the awe that science describes as good for body and mind can be something more: the threshold of prayer, the first word of a conversation with the One who thought it all up. The psalm writers, in fact, did exactly what psychology recommends today: they looked at the sky and let its vastness put their own affairs in proper perspective. One of them wrote that the heavens declare the glory of God and the skies proclaim the work of His hands. And the most personal part is this: the handiwork isn’t only the stars, the kingfishers, and the lotus leaves. You are His handiwork too. Your existence is neither a mistake nor an accident. The psalmist looked at his own body and saw in it the hand of the Creator:

quote.text: For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well.

questions: When was the last time something truly amazed you, and did you give yourself time to take a closer look?
What would change in the way you see yourself if you believed you were someone’s handiwork and not an accident?
Who will you show something this week that amazed you?
